title: You Wanted Healing to Mean You Never Hurt Again. Sometimes Healing Means the Wound No Longer Gets to Rule You.
paragraphs: You Wanted Healing to Mean You Never Hurt Again. Sometimes Healing Means the Wound No Longer Gets to Rule You.
Maybe the miracle you have been waiting for is not that you will forget what happened. Maybe it is that what happened will finally stop deciding who you are.
You thought healing would feel different.
You thought one day you would wake up and it simply would not hurt anymore.
No memories tightening your chest.
No ordinary song suddenly dragging you backward.
No name you still struggle to hear.
No empty chair.
No betrayal replaying itself when the room becomes quiet.
No wondering why you were not enough.
No wondering why God allowed it.
You prayed.
You cried.
You forgave—or at least tried to.
You opened your Bible when you did not feel like opening anything.
You told God things you were almost afraid to say aloud.
And somewhere along the way, you quietly developed a definition of healing:
“If God really heals me, eventually this will stop hurting.”
So when it hurt again, you became afraid.
Maybe I am not healed.
Maybe I did something wrong.
Maybe I did not forgive enough.
Maybe my faith is weak.
Maybe God has forgotten me.
But what if you have been measuring healing by the wrong thing?
What if healing does not always mean the complete erasure of pain?
What if sometimes healing means the pain can knock on the door without being allowed to move back into the house?
Psalm 147:3 says:
“He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds.” — Psalm 147:3, KJV
The Hebrew is breathtaking:
הָרֹפֵא לִשְׁבוּרֵי לֵב וּמְחַבֵּשׁ לְעַצְּבוֹתָם
Ha-rofe lishvurei lev, u-mechabbesh le'atzvotam.
“He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds.”
Notice what Scripture does not say.
It does not shame the brokenhearted for being broken.
It does not tell wounded people that their wounds prove God has abandoned them.
It presents God as the One who comes near to broken hearts and tends their wounds.
That matters.
Because some wounds are not paper cuts.
Some wounds have names.
Some have anniversaries.
Some have court dates.
Some have hospital rooms attached to them.
Some have a grave.
Some have a wedding ring you no longer wear.
Some came from the person who once promised never to hurt you.
Some came from a father who should have protected you.
A mother who should have listened.
A spouse who should have remained faithful.
A friend who knew exactly where you were vulnerable and struck there anyway.
Some wounds came from churches.
Some came from rejection.
Some came from losing someone you begged God to save.
And some came from your own decisions.
Those can be the hardest wounds to carry because there is nobody else to blame.
You remember what you did.
What you said.
What you destroyed.
Who you became.
And sometimes you would give almost anything to go back and stop yourself.
But you cannot.
This is where the Gospel becomes more than a religious slogan.
Jesus did not come merely to teach wounded people how to behave better.
He came for sinners.
He came for the ashamed.
He came for the guilty.
He came for people carrying histories they could not rewrite.
And then He carried sin to the cross.
“He was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities…” — Isaiah 53:5, KJV.
Christian hope is not pretending wounds never happened.
Christian hope is that wounds do not receive the final word.
Jesus does.
That distinction can change everything.
Because perhaps you have been asking God to erase something He has been teaching you to surrender.
You keep praying:
“Lord, make me forget.”
And perhaps the deeper prayer is:
“Lord, even when I remember, do not let this rule me anymore.”
There is a difference.
You can remember without returning.
You can grieve without surrendering your identity to grief.
You can acknowledge what somebody did without allowing what they did to determine what you believe about your worth.
You can forgive without pretending evil was acceptable.
You can establish wise boundaries without living on revenge.
You can miss someone and still keep walking.
You can have tears in your eyes and still be healing.
Healing and hurting are not always opposites.
Sometimes they exist in the same heart.
Think about scars.
A scar does not say there was never a wound.
A scar says the wound did not get the final word.
And this is important: Scripture does not promise that every emotional consequence of suffering disappears immediately when someone trusts Christ.
The Bible repeatedly gives us something more realistic—and, in many ways, more beautiful.
God meets people in suffering.
David could worship while grieving.
Paul could know Christ deeply and still describe himself as troubled, perplexed, persecuted, and struck down—yet “not destroyed” (2 Corinthians 4:8–9).
Even after the resurrection, Jesus showed His disciples the marks in His hands and side (John 20:20).
The risen Christ was victorious.
And the scars were still visible.
Do not push that image farther than Scripture intends, but do not miss its beauty either.
Resurrection did not make Calvary unreal.
Victory did not require pretending the wounds had never existed.
Maybe somebody reading this has been trying to become a person for whom the past never happened.
But you cannot heal by becoming fictional.
God is redeeming the real you.
The you who remembers.
The you who sometimes still cries.
The you who has questions.
The you who can worship on Sunday and struggle on Monday.
The you who thought you were doing better until something triggered the memory again.
The you who feels embarrassed because it has been three years.
Seven years.
Twenty years.
And there are still moments when it hurts.
Listen carefully.
The return of pain does not automatically mean the disappearance of progress.
Sometimes an old wound aches because something touched it.
That does not necessarily mean you are back where you started.
Look at what God has already done.
There was a time when that memory controlled your entire day.
Now perhaps it controls ten minutes.
There was a time when hearing that person's name destroyed you.
Now it hurts, but you recover.
There was a time when anger dictated your decisions.
Now you notice the anger and bring it to Christ.
There was a time when you wanted revenge.
Now you want freedom.
There was a time when you believed what happened to you was who you were.
Now, even with trembling hands, you are beginning to believe what Jesus says about you.
That matters.
Do not despise gradual grace simply because you wanted instantaneous relief.
God's work in us is often deeper than the emotional moment we hoped would fix everything overnight.
There are certainly moments when God brings extraordinary and sudden deliverance.
We should never deny His power to do that.
But Scripture also describes Christian transformation as an ongoing work.
Paul writes that believers are being transformed “from glory to glory” (2 Corinthians 3:18).
There is movement.
Formation.
Growth.
Sanctification.
And sometimes the evidence that Jesus is healing you is not that the battlefield disappeared.
It is that the battlefield no longer owns you.
Maybe you still remember the betrayal.
But you no longer check their profile every night.
Maybe you still miss the person you lost.
But you have begun thanking God for the years you were given instead of only raging over the years you were denied.
Maybe rejection still stings.
But you no longer beg people to choose you in order to believe you have value.
Maybe you still struggle with shame over your past.
But now when shame whispers, “This is who you are,” you answer with the Gospel:
No.
That is what I did.
That is what happened.
That is where I was.
But Jesus Christ has met me there.
The Gospel does not edit your history.
It changes your standing before God and begins transforming what your history gets to mean.
That is the heartbeat of grace.
Peter denied Jesus.
That scandal was real.
Three times.
“I do not know the man.”
Imagine living with that memory.
Imagine remembering the eyes of Jesus after your own mouth denied Him.
But Peter's failure was not the final chapter.
The risen Christ restored him.
“Feed my sheep.” (John 21:17)
Jesus did not pretend Peter had never fallen.
He restored the man who fell.
That is grace.
David had chapters he could never make innocent.
Paul had memories of persecuting Christians that no theological education could erase.
The woman at the well had a relational history Jesus knew completely.
Thomas had doubts.
The thief beside Christ had almost no earthly future left in which to repair his reputation.
Yet again and again, Scripture reveals a Savior who enters human wreckage and does what human beings cannot do for themselves.
He redeems.
He forgives.
He restores.
He makes new.
This is why our message remains:
Not because Jesus changes yesterday into something that never happened.
But because He can change what yesterday is allowed to do with tomorrow.
That is a different kind of miracle.
Maybe you wanted God to remove every reminder.
Instead, He is teaching you that the reminder no longer has authority over your identity.
Maybe you wanted Him to destroy the memory.
Instead, He is removing the memory's throne.
Maybe you wanted never to cry again.
Instead, He is showing you that tears and faith can occupy the same prayer.
Maybe you wanted healing to mean becoming untouched.
But perhaps biblical healing looks more like becoming surrendered.
Held.
Restored.
Changed.
Free.
Not free because nothing hurts.
Free because the hurt is no longer your master.
Jesus is.
And if you are still hurting tonight, please do not turn your pain into evidence that God hates you.
Bring it to Him.
Do not romanticize it.
Do not worship it.
Do not build your identity around it.
Bring it into the light.

There may also be times when healing includes seeking wise pastoral care, trusted Christian community, medical care, or qualified professional counseling. Receiving appropriate help is not inherently evidence of weak faith. God's ordinary provision can include other people carrying burdens with us.
“Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.” — Galatians 6:2, KJV.
You were never commanded to pretend.
You were invited to come.
Jesus said:
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” — Matthew 11:28, KJV.
He did not say:
“Come when you have stopped hurting.”
He did not say:
“Come when your story is respectable.”
He did not say:
“Come after you have repaired yourself.”
Come.
Heavy.
Come.
Exhausted.
Come with the memories.
Come with the anger you are ashamed to admit.
Come with the grief.
Come with the betrayal.
Come with your own sin too.
Because Christianity is not merely the story of victims finding comfort.
It is also the story of sinners finding mercy.
Every one of us ultimately needs more than emotional recovery.
We need reconciliation with God.
Sin separates us from Him, and no amount of positive thinking can remove guilt before a holy God.
That is why Jesus went to the cross.
Christ died for our sins and rose again.
Forgiveness is offered through Him.
Grace is not God saying sin does not matter.
The cross proves it matters terribly.
Grace is God providing in Christ what sinners could never provide for themselves.
So repent.
Turn toward Jesus.
Bring Him the parts of your life you have hidden from everyone else.
Stop trying to negotiate with the darkness.
Stop letting shame convince you that you must clean yourself before approaching the One who cleanses sinners.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9, KJV.
And tomorrow, if the wound aches again, do not immediately declare the healing fake.
Look again.
Is it still ruling you?
Is it still naming you?
Is it still controlling every decision?
Or are you slowly becoming someone who can feel the ache…and still choose Christ?
Someone who can remember…and still worship?
Someone who can grieve…and still love?
Someone who can say:
“That wounded me deeply, but by the grace of Jesus Christ, it will not become my god.”
That is not denial.
That is freedom being learned.
Maybe you know somebody who desperately needs these words.
Someone who thinks they are failing because they are still grieving.
Someone recovering from betrayal.
Someone who keeps asking why healing is taking so long.
Someone who smiles publicly and falls apart privately.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
Not because clicking a button proves your faith. It does not.
We are saved by grace through faith, “not of works, lest any man should boast” (Ephesians 2:8–9).
Send it privately to the person whose grief has lasted longer than everyone else's patience.
Your story does not replace Scripture.
But your testimony can point somebody toward the Savior Scripture reveals.
If this ministry helps you follow Christ, stay close.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend struggling with faith.
Invite the believer who has grown cold.
Invite the seeker who does not know what they believe yet.
Even invite the person who thinks Christianity has nothing left to say to their pain.
You are not required to call evil good in order to heal.
You are not required to erase the person you lost in order to keep living.
You are not required to pretend betrayal did not hurt in order to forgive.
You are not required to become emotionless in order to become faithful.
Bring the wound to Jesus again.
And again.
And again.
Psalm 147:3 does not present God standing impatiently over brokenhearted people asking why they are taking so long.
It presents Him as healer.
הָרֹפֵא לִשְׁבוּרֵי לֵב
Ha-rofe lishvurei lev.
The One healing the brokenhearted.
And maybe that is the sentence you needed tonight.
Not:
“You should be over this by now.”
But:
God is still at work here.
The scar may remain part of your story.
The memory may occasionally still sting.
There may still be days when tears surprise you.
But the wound does not have to sit on the throne anymore.
It does not get to name you.
It does not get to own tomorrow.
It does not get to become your identity.
It does not get to separate you from the love and lordship of Jesus Christ.
Christ gets the throne.
Grace gets the final word.
And perhaps one day you will look at the place you thought would always destroy you and realize something extraordinary:
The wound remained in your memory, but Jesus removed its crown.
Because sometimes the greatest evidence of healing is not that you can no longer feel where you were wounded.
It is that when the wound speaks, you no longer mistake its voice for your master.
Jesus is Lord.
And He is still writing.
